deep_why: The core challenge is that standard recommendation systems treat each item as a string of independent tokens, which blurs the boundaries of what makes one item fundamentally different from another. The underlying principle is that items, not tokens, are the true units of comparison in recommendations—you need to know which tokens belong to the same physical product versus which describe similarities across products. This method works because it partitions attention into two kinds of relationships: within-item (understanding what a single product actually is) and across-item (seeing which products users prefer together), ensuring that the semantic information about each item stays coherent rather than dissolving into token-level patterns that ignore item identity. By respecting items as atomic units, the system can properly measure collaborative preferences (what do users who like item A also like?) without confusing cross-product patterns with product descriptions.

Subtitle translation must simultaneously track who is speaking, maintain consistent terminology across scenes, and preserve the emotional tone needed for an audience to connect with the story. The underlying principle is that these three dimensions of quality are deeply coupled—knowing who speaks shapes what terminology makes sense, and emotional expressiveness depends on getting both speaker identity and terminology right. This framework works because it decomposes the problem into three specialized modules that each solve one coupling point: diarization anchors pronouns and context to the right speaker, terminology identification ensures consistent choices across scenes, and expressiveness enhancement adjusts phrasing to match the original's emotional intent. By addressing these dependencies explicitly rather than treating subtitle translation as generic text translation, the system can preserve the coherence that makes subtitles feel natural rather than mechanical.

Large multimodal systems can reason deeply about why a piece of content matches a query, but running them billions of times per day makes systems too slow to serve real recommendations. The underlying principle is that you can compress sophisticated reasoning from a large system into a smaller, faster system if you teach it not just final rankings but also the confidence calibration and reasoning quality of the original teachers. This distillation works because it captures two kinds of knowledge: what the large models ranked as best (ranking signal) and how sure the large models were about that ranking (calibration signal), allowing a much smaller model to make decisions that align with deep reasoning without performing that reasoning itself. By also fine-tuning only small weights via parameter-efficient methods, the system stays fast enough for production while preserving the trust properties users need—they can see why recommendations were made and believe the system understands their needs.

Combining structured filters (find content from September 2024) with unstructured search (find semantically similar items) creates two problems: either you filter first and miss relevant items that don't perfectly match the constraints, or you search first and then filter, wasting computation on results you'll discard. The underlying principle is that you can avoid this waste by organizing data into subsets where constraints are guaranteed to be consistent—within each subset, all items share the same time period or category. This method works because building search indices on these consistent subsets eliminates imprecision: constraints can eliminate entire subsets upfront without searching them, and the search within each remaining subset focuses on truly relevant candidates rather than later filtering out false matches. By limiting the search scope through this logical subdivision, the system gains both accuracy (no missed results, no false positives) and efficiency (searches don't explore massive irrelevant regions of the data).

Classic advertising auctions assume each ad slot is independent—a person either clicks or doesn't, unaffected by what surrounds it. But when ads are woven into AI-generated text, one ad's presence changes how people perceive others (if one product mention feels natural, a second mention in the same paragraph feels forced, and vice versa). The underlying principle is that when items influence each other's appeal, you must model user choices as probabilistic rankings over all presented options rather than independent decisions. This framework works by formalizing how users mentally rank the options they see: in a cascade model, they read left to right and stop at the first thing that interests them, so earlier positions gain value from blocking later ones; in a logit model, they weigh all options against each other based on context. By explicitly modeling these interaction effects, the auction mechanism can set payments that discourage spam (where redundant ads lower each other's value) while rewarding positions that genuinely enhance the user's experience—solving the real optimization problem rather than an oversimplified independent-slot version.

Every ad shown on a webpage costs users energy—both to download and render the ad code, and to run the tracking systems that let advertisers measure whether the ad was seen or clicked. The underlying principle is that these costs accumulate across billions of daily ad impressions and affect real devices (phones drain battery faster, laptops get hotter), so measuring this externality reveals a hidden expense of the current advertising model. This methodology works by carefully isolating the energy cost of ads through controlled experiments: comparing visits with cookies enabled versus disabled shows consent's cost, comparing visits to real-bidding versus non-real-bidding sites shows tracking's cost, and scaling these measurements across diverse devices shows the impact is real and widespread. By quantifying this overlooked cost, the analysis exposes that the free-content bargain between users and platforms has a tangible physical component—users aren't paying just in privacy but in actual energy consumption, making transparent what the advertisement ecosystem truly costs.

Recommendation systems are shifting from single algorithms choosing products to networks of autonomous agents negotiating with each other—one agent finds candidates, another ranks them, a third negotiates with sellers, a fourth manages transactions. The underlying challenge is that when these agents make independent decisions, failures cascade (a bad ranking output breaks downstream negotiation), emergent behaviors can harm fairness (agents collectively discriminate even without trying), and success looks different to different stakeholders (sellers want revenue, buyers want good deals, platforms want engagement). This framework addresses these challenges by treating the multi-agent system as a coordination problem requiring shared principles: agents must be interpretable (you can trace why they made decisions), robust (failures don't propagate), and aligned with multiple stakeholders' interests simultaneously. By establishing principled evaluation that measures coordination quality rather than just immediate transactions, the workshop enables designing systems where autonomous agents genuinely enhance the marketplace rather than creating hidden harms through emergent interactions.

Search systems represent documents as single dense summaries (a single point in high-dimensional space), but this necessarily loses information—some query terms get emphasized in the summary while others fade, so the ranking quality has a hard ceiling. The underlying principle is that this information loss is partly inevitable (you cannot compress all query-relevant information into a single point) but also partly from something fixable: curse of dimensionality, where high-dimensional spaces make distance calculations meaningless because everything becomes equidistant. This approach works by first acknowledging the hard theoretical limit, then fixing what lies within reach—applying dimensionality reduction (finding the meaningful dimensions and discarding noise) recovers about 7% of lost quality, and combining multiple smaller summaries of the same document rather than one large summary recovers another 2%. By grounding improvements in what's actually solvable given the constraints, the system stops chasing unrealistic performance targets and instead maximizes real-world relevance within the theoretical boundaries of single-document summaries.

Watermarks embedded in image generation models force consistency: if you change any pixel slightly to attack the watermark, the whole image breaks because the generation process is tightly coupled. The underlying principle is that semantic watermarks exploit this—they bind watermarks to high-level image meaning (what the image is about) rather than pixels, so that breaking the watermark requires changing the meaning enough that the image becomes incoherent. But large language models can explore meaning-space systematically: they can reason about what makes an image a 'sunset' and find tiny tweaks to 'sunset-ness' (warming the colors slightly, changing the position of the sun) that keep the image globally coherent while locally disrupting the watermark signal. This attack works because semantic watermarks assume meaning is hard to manipulate precisely, but language models can map meanings to images with enough precision to invalidate that assumption. By exposing this gap, the research reveals that content-aware watermarks need fundamentally different defenses—they cannot rely on tying watermarks to semantic concepts that language models can reason about.

Building production software requires not just writing code but also verifying it works, reviewing it for bugs, and integrating changes with others' work—stages that traditional code-completion tools skip. The underlying principle is that this full pipeline creates a feedback loop: when code is tested and reviewed before merging, developers learn what works and what doesn't, allowing agents to improve continuously rather than generating once and stopping. This tutorial demonstrates how coordination among specialized agents (one writes, one tests, one reviews) combined with persistent memory (the agent recalls what worked before) and runtime feedback (tests show where code broke) lets each stage inform the next. By building tools that agents can call (version control, test runners, code linters), embedding agents into developers' workflows (IDEs, CI/CD pipelines), and measuring success against real engineering criteria (does the code pass review, does it stay performant), agentic development moves from experimental code completion to production-grade software practices.

Web personalization must adapt to users' current interests (this session the user wants winter coats, last month they wanted summer sandals) while remembering what they always prefer (they always favor athletic brands). The underlying principle is that short-term and long-term preferences live at different timescales and require different update speeds: short-term should change quickly (a user's session intent shifts rapidly), long-term should change slowly (core brand preferences stick around), and neither should overwrite the other. This framework works by maintaining two prompts injected into a shared backbone: a fast session-specific prompt tracks current intent via frequent updates, while a slow global prompt anchors to recurring preference patterns learned across all users. By anchoring the slow prompt to prototype patterns refreshed via differentially private federated learning, the system learns from all users' long-term behaviors without storing any individual's history, preserving privacy. By routing queries through these dual timescales, the system balances responsiveness to current needs with stability of core preferences, solving the stability-plasticity tradeoff that makes continual learning hard.

Item representations in recommendation often either describe the item in isolation (using only product attributes) or learn from past behavior (using only what users bought), but these can diverge—a product meant for teenagers might sell well to retirees, so descriptions and actual audience patterns conflict. The underlying principle is that you need both: semantic representations capture the intended identity (what the product is meant to be), but behavioral signals show the lived identity (who actually buys it), and these two must align or recommendations will mismatch what users genuinely want. This approach works by first inferring from item metadata who the product targets (its archetypal audience—the mental profile of ideal buyers), then extracting semantic representations of that archetype, then applying a calibration objective that adjusts these representations to match actual interaction patterns. By grounding generative archetypes in empirical behavior, the system ensures that recommendations reflect reality rather than aspiration: if a formal dress actually appeals to casual dressers, the representation learns that truth, letting recommendations surface the right items to the right users.

Retrieval-augmented systems search a knowledge base to feed documents into language models, improving accuracy by grounding answers in retrieved sources. But adversaries can poison the knowledge base by inserting misleading documents that the retrieval system fetches and hands to the model, corrupting outputs in subtle ways the model cannot detect because it trusts retrieved documents. The underlying principle is that you must validate sources before trusting them: even if a document is retrieved, you should check its credibility against multiple independent knowledge sources to spot poisoned information. This framework works by treating credibility as a network problem—each document has a provenance (who created it, who has shared it), and you can score credibility by propagating trust through this network: documents from trusted sources are credible, documents that contradict trusted sources are suspicious. By using graph-based reasoning to dynamically score which retrieved documents can be trusted, the system detects poisoned additions even when the retrieval mechanism retrieves them, blocking knowledge corruption while preserving legitimate domain expertise that makes retrieval-augmented generation valuable.

Generative models are trained on datasets of examples, but deployed in real applications where data looks different from training (new styles of images, new kinds of text)—this mismatch between training distribution and deployment distribution breaks learned patterns. The underlying principle is that out-of-distribution shifts require adaptation, and adaptation requires two different strategies: for understanding (recognizing what's in a new image), you need techniques that generalize patterns learned during training to new data without forgetting those patterns; for generation (creating images of things not seen during training), you need unified frameworks that can both recognize new concepts and generate them coherently. This tutorial addresses both by surveying how post-training can harden models against distribution shift (adapting existing knowledge to new domains) and how understanding and generation can be unified in frameworks that work across training and deployment distribution gaps. By treating out-of-distribution challenges as fundamental rather than bugs, the research shows how to build generative systems robust enough for complex real-world applications beyond the specific scenarios they saw during training.

Recommendation systems often share expert networks across multiple tasks (predicting clicks, predicting purchases, predicting long-term engagement), where one shared expert helps all tasks by learning general patterns. But some experts end up dominant (high attention from all tasks) while others are ignored (low attention), leaving complementary knowledge unused. The underlying principle is that high-attention and low-attention experts serve different purposes: high-attention experts capture task-specific patterns that directly predict the outcome, while low-attention experts contain auxiliary knowledge that indirectly helps (like knowing user demographics aids predicting both clicks and purchases even if it's not directly predictive). This mechanism works by first identifying which experts are leaders (high gating) versus auxiliary (low gating) through entropy analysis—tasks that struggle (high entropy in their predictions) benefit differently from experts than confident tasks. Then it systematically recycles knowledge from auxiliary experts through multiple lenses: utility (does this expert actually help?), diversity (does it add information not already in leaders?), and task-relatedness (is this knowledge relevant to this particular task?). By treating expert selection as dynamic—adapting which experts matter based on real-time task difficulty—the system gains both accuracy (using all available knowledge) and efficiency (not wasting computation on irrelevant expertise).
